subject: biology
title: BIO1022 practice exam
summary: A full timed practice exam for BIO1022 with six short-answer questions and worked solutions, plus 20 exam-style multiple-choice questions on body plans, plants, physiology, ecology, behaviour and immunity.
body:
This practice exam covers the whole of BIO1022 at the level of a first-year university final exam. Most marks come from applying ideas to data, experiments and unfamiliar organisms, not from recalling definitions alone. Sit it under real conditions, then mark yourself carefully against the worked solutions.

## How to use this practice exam

- **Time limit:** 2 hours in total. Allow about 40 minutes for the 20 multiple-choice questions and about 80 minutes for the short-answer section (roughly 1.5 minutes per mark).
- **Conditions:** closed book, no notes. A basic calculator is allowed. Put your phone in another room.
- **Order:** write your short-answer responses on paper under timed conditions before reading the worked solutions. Then do the multiple-choice questions below.
- **Marking:** the short-answer section is worth 40 marks. Award a mark only when your answer clearly makes the point in the solution. List the topics where you dropped marks and revisit those lessons.
- **Command words:** "describe" means say what happens; "explain" means say what happens and why; "evaluate" means judge strengths and weaknesses; "calculate" means show the formula, substitution, working and units.

## Topics covered

- Animal body plans, protostomes and deuterostomes, major phyla and life histories
- Plant life cycles and major plant groups; fungal structure, nutrition, reproduction and mycorrhizae
- Homeostasis, thermoregulation, osmoregulation, excretion, gas exchange and circulation
- Population growth models, carrying capacity, r and K strategies, community structure, succession and diversity indices
- Competition, predation, mutualism, parasitism and coevolution
- Innate and learned behaviour, optimal foraging, sexual selection and kin selection
- Pathogens, virulence, transmission, R₀ and host–pathogen coevolution
- Innate and adaptive immunity, MHC, antibodies, memory and vaccination

## Short-answer questions

### Question 1 (6 marks)

A newly discovered marine animal has the following features: bilateral symmetry; three germ layers; a body cavity lined completely by mesoderm; a hard outer cuticle that it moults; jointed legs; and, in the embryo, the blastopore becomes the mouth.

(a) State whether the animal is a protostome or a deuterostome, and give the evidence from the description. (2 marks)

(b) Name the type of body cavity and the phylum to which the animal most likely belongs. Justify the phylum with two features. (3 marks)

(c) Name the protostome clade this animal belongs to. (1 mark)

### Question 2 (7 marks)

A desert hopping mouse and a freshwater fish both osmoregulate.

(a) Explain why the freshwater fish produces large volumes of dilute urine. (2 marks)

(b) The hopping mouse excretes urea, but desert birds excrete uric acid. Explain why uric acid is especially suitable for a bird. (2 marks)

(c) A mouse and a lizard of similar mass are kept at 10 °C. The mouse uses about five times more oxygen per gram than the lizard. Explain this difference in terms of thermoregulation. (3 marks)

### Question 3 (8 marks)

Sixty rabbits are released on an island with no predators. Their per capita rate of increase is r = 0.6 per year, and the carrying capacity is estimated at K = 2000.

(a) Using the exponential model Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ, calculate the predicted population after 4 years. (e^2.4 ≈ 11.02) (2 marks)

(b) Using the logistic model, calculate dN/dt when N = 1500. (2 marks)

(c) State the population size at which the logistic model predicts the fastest growth, and calculate that rate. (2 marks)

(d) Some years later, a drought kills 40% of the rabbits regardless of their density, and a disease spreads faster when the rabbits are crowded. Classify each factor and explain your choice for the disease. (2 marks)

### Question 4 (6 marks)

Researchers compared the toxicity of a newt and the resistance of its snake predator in four regions.

| Region | Newt toxin (relative units) | Snake resistance (relative units) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 1 | 1 |
| B | 3 | 2 |
| C | 10 | 9 |
| D | 0 | 1 |

(a) Describe the relationship between newt toxicity and snake resistance. (1 mark)

(b) Explain how a coevolutionary arms race could produce this pattern. (3 marks)

(c) Explain why these data alone do not prove coevolution, and suggest one further piece of evidence that would strengthen the case. (2 marks)

### Question 5 (7 marks)

A new respiratory virus has R₀ = 4 in a fully susceptible population.

(a) Define R₀ and calculate the herd immunity threshold. (3 marks)

(b) A vaccine produces neutralising antibodies. Explain how antibodies can prevent the virus infecting cells. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why a second dose of vaccine given weeks after the first gives a much faster and larger antibody response than the first dose. (2 marks)

### Question 6 (6 marks)

A patient's helper T cells (CD4⁺) are severely depleted by infection.

(a) Explain why the patient's antibody production against most protein antigens falls. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the patient becomes less able to clear virus-infected cells. (2 marks)

(c) State two defences that still function in this patient and explain why they are not directly affected. (2 marks)

## Worked solutions

### Solution 1

(a) **Protostome** (1 mark), because the blastopore becomes the mouth (1 mark).

(b) A cavity fully lined by mesoderm is a **true coelom** (coelomate) (1 mark). The phylum is **Arthropoda** (1 mark): it has jointed legs and a moulted cuticle (exoskeleton); segmentation would also count. Annelids are also coelomate protostomes but lack jointed legs and an exoskeleton (1 mark for two correct features).

(c) **Ecdysozoa**, the moulting protostomes (1 mark).

### Solution 2

(a) The fish's body fluids are hyperosmotic to fresh water, so water constantly enters by osmosis across the gills and skin (1 mark). It must remove this extra water as large volumes of dilute urine, while reabsorbing salts and taking up salt at the gills (1 mark).

(b) Uric acid is non-toxic and almost insoluble, so it can be excreted as a paste with very little water lost, which suits flight weight and dry habitats (1 mark). It can also be stored safely inside a shelled egg during development without poisoning the embryo (1 mark).

(c) The mouse is an **endotherm**: it keeps its body near 37 °C by generating heat metabolically (1 mark). At 10 °C it loses heat quickly to the surroundings, so it must raise its metabolic rate, which uses more oxygen (1 mark). The lizard is an **ectotherm**: its body temperature falls towards 10 °C, so its metabolic rate and oxygen use drop (1 mark).

### Solution 3

(a) Nₜ = N₀eʳᵗ = 60 × e^(0.6 × 4) = 60 × e^2.4 (1 mark) = 60 × 11.02 ≈ **661 rabbits** (1 mark).

(b) dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K = 0.6 × 1500 × (2000 − 1500)/2000 (1 mark) = 900 × 0.25 = **225 rabbits per year** (1 mark).

(c) Fastest at N = K/2 = **1000** (1 mark). dN/dt = rK/4 = 0.6 × 2000 ÷ 4 = **300 rabbits per year** (1 mark).

(d) The drought is **density-independent** because it kills the same proportion whatever the density. The disease is **density-dependent** (1 mark) because crowding increases contact between rabbits, so the transmission rate and the proportion infected rise with density (1 mark).

### Solution 4

(a) Toxin and resistance are **positively correlated**: regions with more toxic newts have more resistant snakes (1 mark).

(b)
- Snakes eating toxic newts select for newts with higher toxin, because more toxic newts survive attacks and reproduce (1 mark).
- More toxic newts in turn select for snakes with heritable resistance, because resistant snakes can eat newts and survive (1 mark).
- This reciprocal selection escalates both traits over generations; where interactions are strongest (region C) both traits reach their highest levels, giving a coevolutionary hotspot (1 mark).

(c) Correlation does not show cause: both traits might respond to a shared third factor such as an environmental condition, or one might change without the other driving it (1 mark). Stronger evidence would be showing that snake resistance is heritable and that the newts' toxin actually reduces snake survival, or genetic data showing toxin-resistance mutations in snakes arose only where toxic newts occur (any one, 1 mark).

### Solution 5

(a) R₀ is the average number of new infections caused by one infected person in a population where everyone is susceptible (1 mark). Threshold = 1 − 1/R₀ = 1 − 1/4 (1 mark) = 0.75, so **75%** of the population must be immune (1 mark).

(b) Neutralising antibodies bind epitopes on the virus surface proteins that the virus uses to attach to host cell receptors (1 mark). The bound antibodies block attachment and entry, and coated viruses are also more easily engulfed by phagocytes (opsonisation) (1 mark).

(c) The first dose triggers a primary response, during which clonal selection produces memory B and T cells specific to the vaccine antigen (1 mark). The second dose activates these memory cells, which are more numerous and respond more quickly, giving a secondary response that is faster, larger and longer-lasting, with more high-affinity antibody (1 mark).

### Solution 6

(a) Most B cells need cytokines and contact from a helper T cell that recognises the same antigen on MHC class II before they can multiply and become plasma cells (1 mark). Without helper T cells, few B cells are activated, so few plasma cells form and antibody production falls (1 mark).

(b) Cytotoxic T cells (CD8⁺) kill infected cells displaying viral peptides on MHC class I (1 mark), but full activation and multiplication of cytotoxic T cells also depends on cytokines from helper T cells, so fewer effective cytotoxic T cells are produced (1 mark).

(c) Any two, with reasons (1 mark each): physical and chemical barriers such as skin and mucus; phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages; natural killer cells; complement; inflammation; interferons. These are innate defences that recognise general features of microbes or damaged cells and do not need T cell help to work.

questions.prompt: Which animal is diploblastic?
questions.explanation: Cnidarians such as jellyfish have only two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm. Flatworms (A) are triploblastic even though they have no body cavity, which makes them a tempting choice. Earthworms and sea stars are triploblastic coelomates.

questions.prompt: A cohort shows very high mortality in the first weeks of life, then a low, steady death rate among survivors. Which life history is most likely?

options.A: Few large offspring with extended parental care
options.C: Many small offspring with little parental care

questions.explanation: Heavy early mortality followed by low mortality is a Type III curve, typical of species producing many small offspring with little care, such as many fish and marine invertebrates. A and B describe species where most individuals survive to old age.

questions.prompt: A nematode and an earthworm differ in their body cavity. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The nematode has a pseudocoelom; the earthworm has a true coelom
options.C: The nematode has a true coelom; the earthworm is acoelomate

questions.explanation: Nematodes have a pseudocoelom, partly lined by mesoderm, while annelids such as earthworms have a coelom fully lined by mesoderm. Acoelomate animals, such as flatworms, have no body cavity at all.

questions.prompt: The leafy green moss plant you see on a damp rock is:
questions.explanation: In bryophytes the gametophyte is the dominant, long-lived generation; the sporophyte is a stalk with a capsule that grows from it and depends on it. A is the common error because in all other land plant groups the visible plant is the sporophyte.

questions.prompt: In angiosperm double fertilisation, what does the second sperm cell form?

options.B: Triploid endosperm, by fusing with two polar nuclei

questions.explanation: One sperm fertilises the egg to form the diploid zygote; the second fuses with the two polar nuclei to make triploid (3n) endosperm, a food store for the embryo. The seed coat develops from maternal tissue, not from a sperm.

questions.prompt: Eucalypt seedlings grown with a mycorrhizal fungus in low-phosphorus soil grow much larger than seedlings without it. What is the best explanation?

options.A: The fungus photosynthesises and gives sugar to the plant
options.B: The fungus fixes atmospheric nitrogen for the plant
options.C: Fungal hyphae explore a far larger soil volume and supply phosphate to the plant
options.D: The fungus kills soil pathogens that would otherwise attack the roots

questions.explanation: Fine hyphae extend well beyond the roots' depletion zone and absorb phosphate, which they pass to the plant in exchange for sugar. A reverses the direction of sugar flow: fungi are heterotrophs. Nitrogen fixation (B) is done by certain bacteria, not mycorrhizal fungi.

questions.prompt: Why does countercurrent flow in fish gills extract more oxygen than if blood and water flowed in the same direction?

options.A: It keeps a concentration gradient favouring diffusion along the whole exchange surface
options.B: It slows the water down so it stays at the gills longer
options.C: It allows oxygen to be actively pumped into the blood
options.D: It mixes oxygenated and deoxygenated blood

questions.explanation: Because the flows run in opposite directions, blood always meets water with a slightly higher oxygen level, so diffusion continues along the whole gill. With parallel flow the two would reach equal concentrations halfway along and transfer would stop. Oxygen moves by diffusion, not active transport.

questions.prompt: Which vertebrate group has a single circulation in which blood passes through the heart once per circuit?
questions.explanation: Fish have a two-chambered heart pumping blood to the gills and then on to the body before it returns: a single circuit. Amphibians have a three-chambered heart with a double circuit, although some mixing occurs in the ventricle. Birds and mammals have fully separated double circulation.

questions.prompt: Body temperature rises above the set point in a mammal. Which response is part of negative feedback?

options.C: Vasodilation of skin arterioles and sweating
options.D: Raising the fur to trap more air

questions.explanation: Negative feedback reverses the change, so the body must lose heat: vasodilation sends more blood to the skin to radiate heat and sweating cools by evaporation. A, B and D all conserve or generate heat and would be responses to cold.

questions.prompt: A population growing logistically has K = 1200. At what population size is its growth rate (dN/dt) greatest?
questions.explanation: In the logistic model, dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K is greatest at N = K/2 = 600, where there are many breeders and resources are still not limiting. At N = K (D) growth stops entirely.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a density-independent factor?

options.A: A frost that kills 30% of insects regardless of their numbers
options.C: Disease spread by contact between individuals
options.D: Predation by a predator that focuses on abundant prey

questions.explanation: A density-independent factor kills the same proportion whatever the density, as frost does. Competition, contact disease and prey-switching predators all have stronger effects per individual when density is higher, so they are density-dependent.

questions.prompt: Two sites each contain 4 species. Site X: 25, 25, 25, 25 individuals. Site Y: 85, 5, 5, 5 individuals. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both sites have equal diversity because richness is equal
options.B: Site Y is more diverse because it has more individuals of one species
options.C: Site X has lower Simpson's diversity because it is more even
options.D: Site X is more diverse because individuals are spread more evenly

questions.explanation: Richness is the same, but diversity indices also account for evenness. Site X is perfectly even, so its Simpson's index is high (about 0.76), while Site Y is dominated by one species (about 0.27). A ignores evenness, which is the most common mistake.

questions.prompt: Where two closely related finch species live on the same island, their beak sizes differ more than where each lives alone. This is best described as:
questions.explanation: Greater divergence of traits where competitors overlap is character displacement: selection favours individuals that use different food, reducing competition. Competitive exclusion (D) would mean one species eliminating the other, but here both coexist.

questions.prompt: A plant provides nectar and shelter to ants, and the ants attack herbivores on the plant. Some ant individuals take nectar but do not defend the plant. These ants are best described as:
questions.explanation: Individuals that take the reward without providing the service are cheaters. Mutualisms are not purely cooperative; each partner benefits from getting more and giving less, which creates conflict. Calling them mutualists (A) ignores that they give no benefit to the plant.

questions.prompt: A shorebird can eat mussels (500 J, handling time 25 s) or crabs (300 J, handling time 10 s). Which prey is more profitable?

options.B: Mussels, because they contain more energy

questions.explanation: Profitability = energy ÷ handling time. Mussels: 500/25 = 20 J s⁻¹. Crabs: 300/10 = 30 J s⁻¹. Crabs are more profitable despite containing less energy. B is the tempting error of comparing total energy and ignoring time.

questions.prompt: Ducklings follow the first moving object they see in the first day or two after hatching, and this attachment lasts. This is:

options.C: A fixed action pattern unaffected by experience

questions.explanation: Learning restricted to a sensitive period early in life and lasting a long time is imprinting. Habituation is a decline in response to a repeated harmless stimulus. It is not purely innate (C), because what the duckling follows depends on what it sees.

questions.prompt: Male elephant seals fight for control of beaches, and a few males father most pups. Which processes are mainly involved?

options.A: Intrasexual selection in a polygynous mating system
options.B: Intersexual selection in a monogamous mating system

questions.explanation: Competition among males for access to females is intrasexual selection, and one male mating with many females is polygyny. Intersexual selection (B) refers to mate choice, and the system is not monogamous.

questions.prompt: When myxoma virus was released in Australia, the original strain was extremely virulent. Over the following years, strains of intermediate virulence became most common. What is the best explanation?

options.A: Viruses always evolve to become harmless to their hosts
options.B: Intermediate strains kept rabbits alive and infectious longer, so they were transmitted more by mosquitoes
options.C: Mosquitoes could not carry highly virulent strains
options.D: Rabbits became immune, so all strains became milder

questions.explanation: Highly virulent strains killed rabbits so quickly that fewer mosquitoes picked them up, so strains that kept hosts alive longer spread more: the virulence–transmission trade-off. A is a common misconception; selection favours maximum transmission, which here meant intermediate, not zero, virulence. Rabbit resistance did evolve too, but that does not explain changes in the virus.

questions.prompt: A disease has R₀ = 10. What proportion of the population must be immune to prevent sustained spread?
questions.explanation: Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R₀ = 1 − 1/10 = 0.9, or 90%. 10% comes from calculating 1/R₀ and forgetting to subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: A mother's antibodies cross the placenta to her fetus. Which description is correct for the baby?

options.A: Active natural immunity with long-lasting memory
options.D: Passive natural immunity that is immediate but short-lived

questions.explanation: The baby receives ready-made antibodies without making its own response, so the immunity is passive; it arises naturally. No memory cells form, so protection fades as the antibodies are broken down over the first months. Active immunity (A) requires the baby's own lymphocytes to respond to an antigen.
